1MBN.claim: Kendrew’s myoglobin: the first protein structure anyone ever saw.
1MBN.prov: Sperm whale, X-ray at 2.0 A. The 1958 model was a 6 A blob that showed only the sausage of the chain; this is the refined coordinate set that came out of the same work. The iron carries a hydroxide — the protein has been oxidised and cannot bind O2 in this state.

1BZP.claim: Deoxy myoglobin: the site with nothing in it.
1BZP.prov: Sperm whale, 1.15 A. The iron sits slightly out of the porphyrin plane, pulled towards the histidine below it. This is the state that is waiting.

1A6M.claim: Oxygen bound: what myoglobin is for.
1A6M.prov: Sperm whale, 1.0 A — among the sharpest protein structures there are. The O2 comes in at an angle and is held there by the distal histidine, which is why the site binds oxygen well and carbon monoxide less well than a bare iron would.

1MBC.claim: Carbon monoxide in the same place: poisoning, as a structure.
1MBC.prov: Sperm whale, 1.5 A. CO binds this site far more tightly than O2 and does not let go, so the protein is full and useless. The distal histidine is what keeps the ratio from being far worse than it is.

1ABS.claim: The same CO, cut loose by light and frozen before it could leave.
1ABS.prov: Sperm whale, 1.5 A at 20 kelvin. A laser broke the Fe-CO bond and the crystal was held cold enough that the CO stopped in a pocket beside the iron instead of escaping. A reaction intermediate, held still and measured.

1YMB.claim: Horse heart myoglobin: another animal, the same answer.
1YMB.prov: X-ray at 1.9 A. About a fifth of the sequence differs from the whale’s and the fold does not care. The residues that do not change are the ones lining the pocket.

2HHB-B.claim: One beta chain of haemoglobin: the same fold, doing a job myoglobin cannot.
2HHB-B.prov: Human, 1.74 A, read from the file hemoglobin-lab already uses. Myoglobin holds oxygen; haemoglobin passes it on, and the difference is not in this chain — it is in having four of them that talk to each other.
